sources.title: Gordon S. Wood, History Lessons
sources.citation: Gordon S. Wood, “History Lessons,” New York Review of Books, 29 March 1984, review of Barbara W. Tuchman, The March of Folly.

verification.note: Complete review body checked at the original publication, with HTML/text retained. Wood praises narrative communication and the Vietnam chapter while criticizing didactic generalization, hindsight and elite explanations. Febvre and the 1973 Burke-edited collection are Wood’s resources, not Tuchman’s debts or a direct posthumous review. Quoted earlier Tuchman essays and the whole March of Folly remain unread; its publisher opening is separately checked. The article’s 1984 date is distinct from profile or footer dates; broad disciplinary diagnoses remain Wood’s judgments.

sources.title: Barbara Tuchman, The March of Folly, publisher opening excerpt
sources.citation: Barbara W. Tuchman, The March of Folly: From Troy to Vietnam (first published 1984), publisher excerpt from the 1985 Random House Trade Paperbacks edition, ISBN 9780345308238, chapter 1 opening.

verification.note: Publisher opening read through the political-philosopher list, Oxenstierna and introduction of Rehoboam. Later excerpt paragraphs and the whole book remain unread. Contemporary recognition, feasible alternatives and collective policy are Tuchman’s stated criteria; they are not independent validation of historical examples. Unnamed historians are not assigned identities. Plato is a substantive but unattainable model; the wider philosopher list does not demonstrate work-specific formative debts. The 1985 edition is not the original publication date.

tuchman_search_excerpt.note: Complete publisher-provided In Search of History excerpt reread, from childhood fiction through the Guns of August weather example; not the entire Practicing History or necessarily the full original lecture. Childhood authors, Babbitt/Lowes/McIlwain courses, the explicitly most formative Widener stacks, Bowen’s reader-turn principle, Macaulay’s formula and qualified Ranke ideal retain their different roles. Emerson/Poe and Pascal are aesthetic/craft examples; Scott/Comines are nested inside the Ranke quotation. Originals were not collated. Existing edge_552 remains; publisher 1982 edition metadata does not newly establish the lecture date.

stone_tuchman_review.note: Official 1978 HTML retained. Selected opening analogy/professional criteria and later merits/explanation passages reread; this does not claim a second whole-body reading. Froissart, Veblen and Geertz are Stone’s interventions, not their direct criticism or Tuchman’s debts. Praise of evidence, restraint and writing coexists with institutional, bourgeois, peasant and explanatory objections. Prior complete-reading scope and edge_554 remain; historical generalizations and forecasts stay attributed.

fox_stone_tuchman_exchange.note: Complete original Fox-Genovese letter and Stone reply reread. Elizabeth challenges status-based dismissal, progress/capitalism assumptions and absent professional disagreement, while defending social groups/material dislocation and expressly denying that Tuchman subscribes to Marxism. Miskimin is her counterexample, not Tuchman’s demonstrated debt. Stone distinguishes research from haute vulgarisation, praises scholarly/prose virtues, qualifies the disaster narrative and invokes Carr as professional reading. Eugene’s books are an analogy, not evidence he authored Elizabeth’s letter. This is reception of a completed 1978 book, not prior influence.
